content.title: About
content.content: Turnips are root vegetables from the Brassicaceae family, cultivated in temperate regions. Raw turnips have a crisp texture, a mildly peppery‑sweet flavor, and a pale white or light purple skin. They are commonly used in salads, as a crunchy snack, or as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnips belong to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and radish.
There are over 200 varieties of turnips, differing in shape, color, and pungency.
Turnips were domesticated in ancient Egypt more than 4,000 years ago.
Both the root and the leafy greens are edible; the greens are often used like spinach.
The purple hue of some turnips comes from anthocyanins, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Turnips provide a good amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in turnips aids digestion and promotes satiety while adding minimal calories.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for cell division and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Anthocyanins and glucosinolates in turnips have anti‑inflammatory and potential anti‑cancer effects.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turnips, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Large amounts of raw turnips can cause gas due to complex sugars.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Because turnips contain vitamin K, they may affect the efficacy of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turnips can be eaten raw in salads, sliced thinly as a snack, or added to sandwiches, soups, and smoothies. For a milder taste, briefly blanch the slices in hot water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store turnips in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp paper towel. Properly stored, they stay fresh for up to two weeks. Remove the leafy tops if they begin to yellow to extend the root's shelf life.
